claim: Neurotransmitters are released at synapses by synaptic vesicles (SVs), which originate from SV precursors (SVPs) that have traveled along the axon.
source: Neurotransmitters are released at synapses by synaptic vesicles (SVs), which originate from SV precursors (SVPs) that have traveled along the axon.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about synaptic vesicle biology and neurotransmitter release.

claim: Each synapse maintains a pool of SVs, only a small fraction of which are released.
source: Because each synapse maintains a pool of SVs, only a small fraction of which are released, it has been thought that axonal transport of SVPs does not affect synaptic function.
evidence: This reflects established understanding in the field about synaptic vesicle pools.

claim: Phosphorylation of the Huntingtin protein (HTT) increases axonal transport of SVPs.
source: Here, studying the corticostriatal network both in microfluidic devices and in mice, we find that phosphorylation of the Huntingtin protein (HTT) increases axonal transport of SVPs and synaptic glutamate release by recruiting the kinesin motor KIF1A.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from microfluidic devices and mouse studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylation of HTT increases synaptic glutamate release by recruiting the kinesin motor KIF1A.
source: Here, studying the corticostriatal network both in microfluidic devices and in mice, we find that phosphorylation of the Huntingtin protein (HTT) increases axonal transport of SVPs and synaptic glutamate release by recruiting the kinesin motor KIF1A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased glutamate release and KIF1A recruitment in HTT-SD mice.

claim: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation causes SV over-accumulation at synapses in mice.
source: In mice, constitutive HTT phosphorylation causes SV over-accumulation at synapses, increases the probability of SV release, and impairs motor skill learning on the rotating rod.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data showing increased SV numbers at corticostriatal synapses in HTT-SD mice.

claim: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation increases the probability of SV release.
source: In mice, constitutive HTT phosphorylation causes SV over-accumulation at synapses, increases the probability of SV release, and impairs motor skill learning on the rotating rod.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing altered short-term plasticity in HTT-SD mice.

claim: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation impairs motor skill learning on the rotating rod.
source: In mice, constitutive HTT phosphorylation causes SV over-accumulation at synapses, increases the probability of SV release, and impairs motor skill learning on the rotating rod.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from rotarod experiments showing impaired learning in HTT-SD mice.

claim: Silencing KIF1A in HTT-SD mice restored SV transport to wild-type levels.
source: Silencing KIF1A in these mice restored SV transport and motor skill learning to wild-type levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that sh-Kif1a treatment normalized SV transport in HTT-SD mice.

claim: Silencing KIF1A in HTT-SD mice restored motor skill learning to wild-type levels.
source: Silencing KIF1A in these mice restored SV transport and motor skill learning to wild-type levels.
evidence: This is supported by rotarod behavioral data showing improved performance in HTT-SD mice treated with sh-Kif1a.

claim: Axonal SVP transport within the corticostriatal network influences synaptic plasticity.
source: Axonal SVP transport within the corticostriatal network thus influences synaptic plasticity and motor skill learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing that manipulating SVP transport affects short-term plasticity.

claim: Axonal SVP transport within the corticostriatal network influences motor skill learning.
source: Axonal SVP transport within the corticostriatal network thus influences synaptic plasticity and motor skill learning.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that manipulating SVP transport affects rotarod performance.

claim: SVs begin life as SV precursors (SVPs), which are formed in the cell body and transported along the axon to the presynapse.
source: SVs actually begin life as SV precursors (SVPs), which are formed in the cell body and transported along the axon to the presynapse—a distance that can span meters (Guedes-Dias and Holzbaur, 2019; Rizalar et al., 2021; Rizzoli, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on SVP transport.

claim: The distance from cell body to presynapse can span meters.
source: SVs actually begin life as SV precursors (SVPs), which are formed in the cell body and transported along the axon to the presynapse—a distance that can span meters (Guedes-Dias and Holzbaur, 2019; Rizalar et al., 2021; Rizzoli, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about axon length, supported by citations.

claim: Synaptic SV pools contain hundreds of vesicles of which only a few percent participate in synaptic release.
source: It is thought that the synaptic SV pools, which contain hundreds of vesicles of which only a few percent participate in synaptic release (Reshetniak and Rizzoli, 2021), are sufficient to ensure a ready supply of SVs to be released, even with prolonged neuronal stimulation (Denker et al., 2011; Rizzoli, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on synaptic vesicle pools.

claim: Synaptic SV pools are sufficient to ensure a ready supply of SVs to be released, even with prolonged neuronal stimulation.
source: It is thought that the synaptic SV pools, which contain hundreds of vesicles of which only a few percent participate in synaptic release (Reshetniak and Rizzoli, 2021), are sufficient to ensure a ready supply of SVs to be released, even with prolonged neuronal stimulation (Denker et al., 2011; Rizzoli, 2014).
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Neighboring synapses can draw on local SV pools that circulate between them.
source: If necessary, neighboring synapses can draw on local SV pools that circulate between them (Wong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, null mutants for the kinesin-related gene unc-104 lead to defects in SVP transport.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, null mutants for the kinesin-related gene unc-104 or the vesicle-associated protein SAM-4 lead to defects in SVP transport, with a consequent lack of SVs at synapses and locomotor deficits (Hall and Hedgecock, 1991; Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in C. elegans.

claim: In C. elegans, null mutants for unc-104 result in a lack of SVs at synapses and locomotor deficits.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, null mutants for the kinesin-related gene unc-104 or the vesicle-associated protein SAM-4 lead to defects in SVP transport, with a consequent lack of SVs at synapses and locomotor deficits (Hall and Hedgecock, 1991; Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In Drosophila, deletion of the imac gene impairs SVP axonal transport and the formation of synaptic boutons.
source: In Drosophila, deletion of the imac gene, a kinesin-3 family member, impairs SVP axonal transport and the formation of synaptic boutons (Pack-Chung et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research in Drosophila.

claim: KIF1A is the mammalian homologue of unc-104.
source: In mice, loss of function of unc-104's mammalian homologue, KIF1A (Okada et al., 1995), leads to the accumulation of SVPs in the cell body and a dramatic reduction in the number of SVs at synapses, along with sensorimotor deficits and early postnatal death (Yonekawa et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Loss of function of KIF1A in mice leads to the accumulation of SVPs in the cell body.
source: In mice, loss of function of unc-104's mammalian homologue, KIF1A (Okada et al., 1995), leads to the accumulation of SVPs in the cell body and a dramatic reduction in the number of SVs at synapses, along with sensorimotor deficits and early postnatal death (Yonekawa et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Loss of function of KIF1A in mice leads to a dramatic reduction in the number of SVs at synapses.
source: In mice, loss of function of unc-104's mammalian homologue, KIF1A (Okada et al., 1995), leads to the accumulation of SVPs in the cell body and a dramatic reduction in the number of SVs at synapses, along with sensorimotor deficits and early postnatal death (Yonekawa et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Loss of function of KIF1A in mice leads to sensorimotor deficits and early postnatal death.
source: In mice, loss of function of unc-104's mammalian homologue, KIF1A (Okada et al., 1995), leads to the accumulation of SVPs in the cell body and a dramatic reduction in the number of SVs at synapses, along with sensorimotor deficits and early postnatal death (Yonekawa et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: HTT plays a prominent role in axonal transport.
source: Mice bearing mutations in Huntingtin (HTT), a protein that plays a prominent role in axonal transport (Saudou and Humbert, 2016), provide one model system that could illuminate the role of SVP transport on synaptic homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: HTT scaffolds various cargoes including endosomes, autophagosomes, and vesicles containing BDNF and APP.
source: HTT scaffolds various cargoes—endosomes, autophagosomes, vesicles containing BDNF, APP, etc. (Bruyère et al., 2020; Cason et al., 2021; Caviston et al., 2011; Fu and Holzbaur, 2014; Gauthier et al., 2004; Her and Goldstein, 2008; Liot et al., 2013; Wong and Holzbaur, 2014)—along with the appropriate molecular motors for anterograde or retrograde transport and any adaptor proteins that may be needed.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The direction of HTT-mediated transport is dictated by its phosphorylation at serine 421.
source: Because the direction of HTT-mediated transport is dictated by its phosphorylation at serine 421 (Bruyère et al., 2020; Colin et al., 2008; Ehinger et al., 2020; Vitet et al., 2020), we were able to investigate how mutations at this site affect axonal transport of SVPs.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the anterograde velocity of VAMP2-positive vesicles.
source: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the anterograde velocity of VAMP2-positive vesicles (Figure 1B, left graph), the number of anterograde vesicles, and the linear flow rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), leading to an increase in the net directional flux of VAMP2-mCherry vesicles traveling toward the presynapse (Figure 1B, right graph).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the number of anterograde VAMP2-positive vesicles.
source: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the anterograde velocity of VAMP2-positive vesicles (Figure 1B, left graph), the number of anterograde vesicles, and the linear flow rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), leading to an increase in the net directional flux of VAMP2-mCherry vesicles traveling toward the presynapse (Figure 1B, right graph).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the linear flow rate of VAMP2-positive vesicles.
source: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the anterograde velocity of VAMP2-positive vesicles (Figure 1B, left graph), the number of anterograde vesicles, and the linear flow rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), leading to an increase in the net directional flux of VAMP2-mCherry vesicles traveling toward the presynapse (Figure 1B, right graph).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the net directional flux of VAMP2-mCherry vesicles traveling toward the presynapse.
source: Constitutive HTT phosphorylation (S421D) increased the anterograde velocity of VAMP2-positive vesicles (Figure 1B, left graph), the number of anterograde vesicles, and the linear flow rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), leading to an increase in the net directional flux of VAMP2-mCherry vesicles traveling toward the presynapse (Figure 1B, right graph).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was no significant effect of HTT-SA mutation on VAMP2-mCherry vesicle velocities or net directional flux in axons.
source: There was no significant effect on VAMP2-mCherry vesicle velocities or net directional flux of HTT-SA mutation in axons (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The frequency of VGLUT1-pHluorin release events at synapses was significantly greater in HTT-SD neurons.
source: The amplitude of VGLUT1 events was similar in WT, HTT-SA, and HTT-SD neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), but the frequency of release events at synapses was significantly greater only in HTT-SD neurons (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The amplitude of VGLUT1 events was similar in WT, HTT-SA, and HTT-SD neurons.
source: The amplitude of VGLUT1 events was similar in WT, HTT-SA, and HTT-SD neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), but the frequency of release events at synapses was significantly greater only in HTT-SD neurons (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HTT-SD and HTT-SA mice showed no differences from WT in motor coordination.
source: We had previously characterized HTT-SA, HTT-SD, and WT mice and found no differences between them in motor coordination (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), forelimb strength (grip test), or anxious-depressive behavior (in the elevated plus maze test) (Ehinger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by previous experimental data cited from Ehinger et al., 2020 and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HTT-SD and HTT-SA mice showed no differences from WT in forelimb strength (grip test).
source: We had previously characterized HTT-SA, HTT-SD, and WT mice and found no differences between them in motor coordination (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), forelimb strength (grip test), or anxious-depressive behavior (in the elevated plus maze test) (Ehinger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by previous experimental data cited from Ehinger et al., 2020.

claim: HTT-SD and HTT-SA mice showed no differences from WT in anxious-depressive behavior (in the elevated plus maze test).
source: We had previously characterized HTT-SA, HTT-SD, and WT mice and found no differences between them in motor coordination (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), forelimb strength (grip test), or anxious-depressive behavior (in the elevated plus maze test) (Ehinger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by previous experimental data cited from Ehinger et al., 2020.

claim: WT mice nearly doubled their latency to fall over the first 3 days/30 sessions of rotarod training.
source: Over the 8 days, the WT mice nearly doubled their latency to fall over the first 3 days/30 sessions of training (the learning phase) and then maintained that skill (the consolidation phase) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: HTT-SD mice did not improve as much as WT during the initial learning phase of rotarod training and plateaued at a lower level of skill.
source: The HTT-SD mice did not improve as much during the initial learning phase and plateaued at a lower level of skill.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: HTT-SA mice learned more gradually than WT on the rotarod but by the eighth day were virtually equivalent.
source: The HTT-SA mice learned much more gradually than WT but by the eighth day were virtually equivalent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Motor skill learning relies on communication between the dorsal striatum and layer V pyramidal neurons in the motor cortex via the release of glutamate by the cortical afferences.
source: Motor skill learning relies on communication between the dorsal striatum and layer V pyramidal neurons in the motor cortex via the release of glutamate by the cortical afferences (Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Jin and Costa, 2015; Perrin and Venance, 2019; Yin and Knowlton, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: HTT-SD mice did not differ from WT or HTT-SA mice in sEPSC amplitude or frequency.
source: The HTT-SD mice did not differ from WT or HTT-SA mice in sEPSC amplitude or frequency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In WT mice, corticostriatal short-term plasticity was facilitated for short ISIs (25 and 50 ms), with a lack of significant plasticity at 100 ms followed by a short-term depression for longer ISIs (250 and 500 ms).
source: Paired-pulse ratio (PPR) analysis revealed that in WT mice, corticostriatal short-term plasticity was facilitated for short ISIs (25 and 50 ms), with a lack of significant plasticity at 100 ms followed by a short-term depression for longer ISIs (250 and 500 ms), as previously described (Goubard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to previous research.

claim: In HTT-SD mice, there was no short-term facilitation but only depression starting from 100 ms ISIs.
source: In HTT-SD mice, there was no short-term facilitation but only depression starting from 100 ms ISIs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: HTT-SA mice showed a short-term plasticity similar to WT mice, except that the facilitation expression window widened up to 100 ms ISIs.
source: HTT-SA mice showed a short-term plasticity similar to WT mice, except that the facilitation expression window widened up to 100 ms ISIs (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The lower facilitation in HTT-SD MSNs indicates that constitutive phosphorylation of HTT increases the probability of glutamate release in pyramidal cells.
source: The lower facilitation in HTT-SD MSNs indicates that constitutive phosphorylation of HTT increases the probability of glutamate release in pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiological data showing altered short-term plasticity.

claim: Decreased facilitation could indicate changes in the number of SVs at the presynapse.
source: Since decreased facilitation could indicate changes in the number of SVs at the presynapse (Park et al., 2012; Pulido and Marty, 2017), we investigated the number of SVs at axon terminals within the corticostriatal network using electron microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: With chronic HTT phosphorylation (HTT-SD mice), the number of synapses did not change.
source: With chronic HTT phosphorylation (HTT-SD mice), the number of synapses did not change (Figure 4Bi) but there were a greater number of SVs at the axon terminals than in WT mice (Figure 4Bii).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4Bi.

claim: With chronic HTT phosphorylation (HTT-SD mice), there were a greater number of SVs at the axon terminals than in WT mice.
source: With chronic HTT phosphorylation (HTT-SD mice), the number of synapses did not change (Figure 4Bi) but there were a greater number of SVs at the axon terminals than in WT mice (Figure 4Bii).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4Bii.

claim: The presynaptic size was smaller in the HTT-SD corticostriatal synapses.
source: The presynaptic size was smaller in the HTT-SD corticostriatal synapses (Figure 4Biii), leading to an increase in SV density in HTT-SD presynaptic terminals (Figure 4Biv).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4Biii.

claim: HTT-SD presynaptic terminals have an increased SV density.
source: The presynaptic size was smaller in the HTT-SD corticostriatal synapses (Figure 4Biii), leading to an increase in SV density in HTT-SD presynaptic terminals (Figure 4Biv).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4Biv.

claim: HTT-SD axon terminals exhibited a greater density of SVs in the most distal zone (zone 3).
source: There was no difference between the genotypes in terms of the area of the zones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), but HTT-SD axon terminals exhibited a greater density of SVs in the most distal zone (zone 3) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: HTT-SA axon terminals had fewer vesicles than WT.
source: The fact that HTT-SA axon terminals had fewer vesicles lends further support to this explanation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: KIF1A is in the proteome of HTT-associated vesicles.
source: We observed KIF1A in the proteome of HTT-associated vesicles (Figure 5A; Migazzi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A and cited from Migazzi et al., 2021.

claim: KIF1A colocalizes with HTT immunopositive puncta in free-cultured cortical neurons at DIV 5.
source: We found that KIF1A colocalizes with HTT immunopositive puncta in free-cultured cortical neurons at DIV 5 using a two-dimensional stimulated emission depletion (2D-STED) super-resolution microscope (Figure 5B, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by 2D-STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is greater colocalization of HTT with KIF1A and VAMP2 in HTT-SD neuronal circuits than in WT.
source: We assessed this possibility by permeabilizing isolated axons within the distal part of microfluidic axonal compartments and, using Airyscan confocal high-resolution microscopy, we observed greater colocalization of HTT with KIF1A and VAMP2 in HTT-SD neuronal circuits than in WT (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Airyscan microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is a significantly greater PLA signal for HTT-KIF1A interaction in HTT-SD neurons.
source: We then used proximity ligation assay (PLA) to confirm the in cellulo interaction between HTT and KIF1A. We observed a significantly greater PLA signal in HTT-SD neurons (Figure 5D), despite no change in PLA levels of VAMP2 with HTT and KIF1A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: HTT-SD showed a greater vesicular/cytosolic ratio for KIF1A.
source: Finally, we prepared vesicular-enriched fractions from WT and HTT-SD mouse brains and immunoblotted them for KIF1A. HTT-SD showed a greater vesicular/cytosolic ratio for KIF1A (Figure 5E), while p150 remained constant and the total brain levels of KIF1A did not differ between the genotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The total brain levels of KIF1A did not differ between WT and HTT-SD genotypes.
source: Finally, we prepared vesicular-enriched fractions from WT and HTT-SD mouse brains and immunoblotted them for KIF1A. HTT-SD showed a greater vesicular/cytosolic ratio for KIF1A (Figure 5E), while p150 remained constant and the total brain levels of KIF1A did not differ between the genotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Silencing KIF1A in WT cortical neurons decreased VAMP2 anterograde vesicle velocity.
source: We found that silencing KIF1A in WT cortical neurons decreased VAMP2 anterograde vesicle velocity, the number of anterograde vesicles (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), the linear flow (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), and the net directional flux of VAMP2 vesicles toward the axon terminals (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Silencing KIF1A in HTT-SD reduced the anterograde velocity of VAMP2 vesicles close to values observed in WT neurons.
source: Silencing KIF1A in HTT-SD reduced the anterograde velocity of VAMP2 vesicles close to values observed in WT neurons (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: KIF1A silencing reduced the number of anterograde vesicles, linear flow, and net directional flux in HTT-SD to values found in WT.
source: KIF1A silencing also reduced the number of anterograde vesicles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), linear flow, and net directional flux in HTT-SD to values found in WT (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The velocity and number of retrograde-moving VAMP2 vesicles was lower in HTT-SD neurons after KIF1A silencing.
source: The velocity and number of retrograde-moving VAMP2 vesicles was also lower in HTT-SD neurons (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: KIF1A has a reported role as a dynein activator.
source: This attenuation of retrograde transport might be linked to KIF1A's reported role as a dynein activator (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Chronic HTT phosphorylation increased the anterograde transport, the linear flow, and the net directional flux of BDNF-containing vesicles.
source: Chronic HTT phosphorylation increased the anterograde transport, the linear flow, and the net directional flux of BDNF-containing vesicles, in agreement with previous studies (Colin et al., 2008; Ehinger et al., 2020; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and citations to previous studies.

claim: Silencing KIF1A did not affect BDNF dynamics either in WT or in HTT-SD neurons.
source: Silencing KIF1A did not affect BDNF dynamics either in WT or in HTT-SD neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The phospho-HTT-dependent increase in SVP anterograde transport, in contrast to BDNF, is mediated by KIF1A.
source: This indicates that the phospho-HTT-dependent increase in SVP anterograde transport, in contrast to BDNF, is mediated by KIF1A.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of KIF1A silencing on VAMP2 vs. BDNF transport.

claim: WT sh-Kif1a presynapses showed significantly fewer SVs than WT sh-Scr presynapses.
source: WT sh-Kif1a presynapses showed significantly fewer SVs than WT sh-Scr presynapses (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The number of SVs at presynapses in HTT-SD brains treated with sh-Kif1a reverted to WT levels.
source: As previously shown (Figure 4B), there were significantly more SVs at presynapses in HTT-SD, but this number reverted to WT levels in HTT-SD brains treated with sh-Kif1a (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Decreasing the phospho-HTT-mediated anterograde transport of SVPs by reducing KIF1A levels in corticostriatal-projecting neurons reduces the number of SVs at presynapses.
source: These data demonstrate that decreasing the phospho-HTT-mediated anterograde transport of SVPs by reducing KIF1A levels in corticostriatal-projecting neurons reduces the number of SVs at presynapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that sh-Kif1a treatment reduces SV numbers.

claim: There is a close relationship between axonal transport and synaptic SV content.
source: This in turn indicates a close relationship between axonal transport and synaptic SV content.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing that manipulating axonal transport affects SV numbers at synapses.

claim: Silencing KIF1A improved the performance of HTT-SD mice on the rotarod over the first 6 days.
source: HTT-SD mice did not show much improvement over 8 days (Figure 8B), as with the non-injected mice (Figure 2B). Silencing KIF1A improved the performance of the HTT-SD mice over the first 6 days, but then the mice seemed to lose ground (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by rotarod behavioral data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The improvement in motor learning of the HTT-SD mice via sh-Kif1a silencing was significant on the first day of training, but the effect did not last until the eighth day.
source: Indeed, the improvement in motor learning of the HTT-SD mice via sh-Kif1a silencing was significant on the first day of training, but the effect did not last until the eighth day (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by rotarod behavioral data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs in the corticostriatal projecting neurons influences the number of SVs at synapses.
source: Nonetheless, these findings indicate that HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs in the corticostriatal projecting neurons, a process modulated by phosphorylation, influences the number of SVs at synapses, the probability of release, and the efficacy of motor skill learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data showing that manipulating the HTT-KIF1A pathway affects SV numbers.

claim: HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs in the corticostriatal projecting neurons influences the probability of release.
source: Nonetheless, these findings indicate that HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs in the corticostriatal projecting neurons, a process modulated by phosphorylation, influences the number of SVs at synapses, the probability of release, and the efficacy of motor skill learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data showing that manipulating the HTT-KIF1A pathway affects short-term plasticity.

claim: HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs in the corticostriatal projecting neurons influences the efficacy of motor skill learning.
source: Nonetheless, these findings indicate that HTT-KIF1A-mediated axonal transport of SVPs in the corticostriatal projecting neurons, a process modulated by phosphorylation, influences the number of SVs at synapses, the probability of release, and the efficacy of motor skill learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data showing that manipulating the HTT-KIF1A pathway affects rotarod performance.

claim: The anterograde transport of SVP is driven predominantly by the kinesin-3 motor KIF1A.
source: The anterograde transport of SVP is driven predominantly by the kinesin-3 motor KIF1A (Guedes-Dias and Holzbaur, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: HTT and KIF1A interactomes suggested a possible interaction between the two proteins.
source: HTT and KIF1A interactomes suggested a possible interaction between the two proteins (Shirasaki et al., 2012; Stucchi et al., 2018), but this had not been tested.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Axonal transport of SVPs influences synaptic function.
source: We show here that axonal transport of SVPs influences synaptic function.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HTT's phosphorylation status fine-tunes SVP transport efficiency through its recruitment of KIF1A.
source: Specifically, HTT's phosphorylation status fine-tunes SVP transport efficiency through its recruitment of KIF1A.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing that HTT phosphorylation affects KIF1A recruitment and SVP transport.

claim: Genetically blocking dephosphorylation at S421 impaired motor learning.
source: Genetically blocking dephosphorylation at S421 impaired motor learning, and abolishing KIF1A activity in the context of constitutive phosphorylation only partially restored motor performance on the rotarod.
evidence: This is supported by rotarod behavioral data from HTT-SD mice.

claim: Abolishing KIF1A activity in the context of constitutive phosphorylation only partially restored motor performance on the rotarod.
source: Genetically blocking dephosphorylation at S421 impaired motor learning, and abolishing KIF1A activity in the context of constitutive phosphorylation only partially restored motor performance on the rotarod.
evidence: This is supported by rotarod behavioral data from HTT-SD mice treated with sh-Kif1a.

claim: DENN/MADD, a Rab3-GEP that binds to KIF1A (and KIF1Bß), regulates SVP binding to microtubules according to Rab3's nucleotide state.
source: This work places HTT among the proteins that participate in SVP transport (Guedes-Dias and Holzbaur, 2019) and closes a loop opened by the discovery that DENN/MADD, a Rab3-GEP that binds to KIF1A (and KIF1Bß), regulates SVP binding to microtubules according to Rab3's nucleotide state (Niwa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Rab3 is part of the HTT interactome.
source: Rab3 is part of the HTT interactome (Shirasaki et al., 2012) and enriched in SVs (Takamori et al., 2006); previous work in Drosophila larval axons showed that reducing HTT levels decreases the transport of Rab3-positive vesicles (White et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Rab3 is enriched in SVs.
source: Rab3 is part of the HTT interactome (Shirasaki et al., 2012) and enriched in SVs (Takamori et al., 2006); previous work in Drosophila larval axons showed that reducing HTT levels decreases the transport of Rab3-positive vesicles (White et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Reducing HTT levels decreases the transport of Rab3-positive vesicles in Drosophila larval axons.
source: Rab3 is part of the HTT interactome (Shirasaki et al., 2012) and enriched in SVs (Takamori et al., 2006); previous work in Drosophila larval axons showed that reducing HTT levels decreases the transport of Rab3-positive vesicles (White et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In the context of Huntington disease (HD), both Rab3 levels and the conversion from GTP to GDP state are dysregulated.
source: In the context of Huntington disease (HD), which is caused by polyglutamine expansions in HTT, both Rab3 levels and the conversion from GTP to GDP state are dysregulated, which is consistent with a role for HTT in the transport of SVPs.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about HD pathology.

claim: Studies in HD models have revealed alterations in HTT phosphorylation at S421 that could result from defects in Akt, the S421 kinase, or dysregulation of the phosphatases calcineurin (PP2B) and PP2A.
source: Studies in HD models have revealed alterations in HTT phosphorylation at S421 that could result from defects in Akt, the S421 kinase, or dysregulation of the phosphatases calcineurin (PP2B) and PP2A (Humbert et al., 2002; Metzler et al., 2010; Pardo et al., 2006; Warby et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Promoting HTT phosphorylation is neuroprotective, as it restores the transport and release of BDNF.
source: That such a study would be worthwhile is suggested by the fact that promoting HTT phosphorylation is neuroprotective, as it restores the transport and release of BDNF (Humbert et al., 2002; Kratter et al., 2016; Pardo et al., 2006; Pineda et al., 2009; Warby et al., 2009; Zala et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Release of glutamate at the corticostriatal synapse is altered in HD brains-on-chips.
source: It is interesting to note in this context that release of glutamate at the corticostriatal synapse is altered in HD brains-on-chips (Virlogeux et al., 2018) and in vivo (Fernández-García et al., 2020; Smith-Dijak et al., 2019) and that stimulating glutamatergic corticostriatal connections in HD reverses motor symptoms in HD mice (Fernández-García et al., 2020), suggesting that reestablishment of glutamate synaptic release capacities could have therapeutic potential.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Release of glutamate at the corticostriatal synapse is altered in vivo in HD.
source: It is interesting to note in this context that release of glutamate at the corticostriatal synapse is altered in HD brains-on-chips (Virlogeux et al., 2018) and in vivo (Fernández-García et al., 2020; Smith-Dijak et al., 2019) and that stimulating glutamatergic corticostriatal connections in HD reverses motor symptoms in HD mice (Fernández-García et al., 2020), suggesting that reestablishment of glutamate synaptic release capacities could have therapeutic potential.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Reestablishment of glutamate synaptic release capacities could have therapeutic potential in HD.
source: It is interesting to note in this context that release of glutamate at the corticostriatal synapse is altered in HD brains-on-chips (Virlogeux et al., 2018) and in vivo (Fernández-García et al., 2020; Smith-Dijak et al., 2019) and that stimulating glutamatergic corticostriatal connections in HD reverses motor symptoms in HD mice (Fernández-García et al., 2020), suggesting that reestablishment of glutamate synaptic release capacities could have therapeutic potential.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the cited research.

claim: Genetically impairing KIF1A reduces the number of SVs at nerve terminals and causes postnatal lethality.
source: Indeed, genetically impairing KIF1A reduces the number of SVs at nerve terminals and causes postnatal lethality (Yonekawa et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: KIF1A loss-of-function variants are associated with four diseases: autosomal recessive hereditary sensory neuropathy IIC, autosomal dominant mental retardation (ADMR) type 9, autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia type 30, and autosomal dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP).
source: KIF1A loss-of-function variants, most of them located within the conserved motor domain, reduce SVP transport and are associated with four diseases: autosomal recessive hereditary sensory neuropathy IIC, autosomal dominant mental retardation (ADMR) type 9, autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia type 30, and autosomal dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) (Pennings et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The KIF1A gain-of-function mutation V8M causes another type of HSP and leads to greater anterograde transport of vesicles and abnormal accumulation of vesicles at synapses.
source: This is consistent with the fact that the KIF1A gain-of-function mutation V8M, which causes another type of HSP, leads to greater anterograde transport of vesicles and abnormal accumulation of vesicles at synapses (Chiba et al., 2019; Gabrych et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Point mutations in the autoinhibitory domain of unc-104 cause hyperactive axonal transport and abnormal accumulation of SVs.
source: Further evidence for the sensitivity of synapses to both too little and too much SVPs comes from point mutations in the autoinhibitory domain of unc-104 that cause hyperactive axonal transport and abnormal accumulation of SVs (Cong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Depletion of kinesin-binding protein, KBP, which inhibits KIF1A activity, leads to the abnormal accumulation of both KIF1A and vesicles at neurite terminals.
source: Similarly, depletion of kinesin-binding protein, KBP, which inhibits KIF1A activity, leads to the abnormal accumulation of both KIF1A and vesicles at neurite terminals (Kevenaar et al., 2016), and nonsense mutations of KBP cause Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome (also called marfanoid-craniosynostosis syndrome), which is characterized by intellectual disability, skeletal abnormalities, and axonal neuropathy (Dafsari et al., 2015; Valence et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Nonsense mutations of KBP cause Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome, which is characterized by intellectual disability, skeletal abnormalities, and axonal neuropathy.
source: Similarly, depletion of kinesin-binding protein, KBP, which inhibits KIF1A activity, leads to the abnormal accumulation of both KIF1A and vesicles at neurite terminals (Kevenaar et al., 2016), and nonsense mutations of KBP cause Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome (also called marfanoid-craniosynostosis syndrome), which is characterized by intellectual disability, skeletal abnormalities, and axonal neuropathy (Dafsari et al., 2015; Valence et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Within the presynapse, SVs are organized into different pools—the RRP, the recycling pool, and the RP—according to their composition, age, and distance from the active zone.
source: Within the presynapse, SVs are organized into different pools—the RRP, the recycling pool, and the RP—according to their composition, age, and distance from the active zone (Crawford and Kavalali, 2015; Kaeser and Regehr, 2017; Rizzoli, 2014; Truckenbrodt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The RRP contains the SVs ready to be released upon neural activity and is thought to be refilled by SVs from the RP by a slow process (hundreds of milliseconds).
source: The RRP contains the SVs ready to be released upon neural activity and is thought to be refilled by SVs from the RP by a slow process (hundreds of milliseconds) (Pulido and Marty, 2017; Rizzoli, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Vesicles are most likely to accumulate where the SVPs detach from the KIF1A motor, away from the membrane and the active zone.
source: This is consistent with the fact that vesicles are most likely to accumulate where the SVPs detach from the KIF1A motor, away from the membrane and the active zone (Bodaleo and Gonzalez-Billault, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Newly produced vesicles arriving at the presynaptic zone are preferentially released.
source: In addition, newly produced vesicles arriving at the presynaptic zone are preferentially released (Truckenbrodt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The locations of SV populations relative to the membrane do not reliably define vesicular pool identities.
source: Although the locations of SV populations relative to the membrane do not reliably define vesicular pool identities (Denker et al., 2009; Fernandez-Alfonso and Ryan, 2008; Fredj and Burrone, 2009), we propose that this population distal from the membrane influences the replenishment of the pools nearer the membrane, that is, the RRP (Kidokoro et al., 2004) and/or the recycling pool (Ratnayaka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The population of SVs distal from the membrane influences the replenishment of the pools nearer the membrane, that is, the RRP and/or the recycling pool.
source: Although the locations of SV populations relative to the membrane do not reliably define vesicular pool identities (Denker et al., 2009; Fernandez-Alfonso and Ryan, 2008; Fredj and Burrone, 2009), we propose that this population distal from the membrane influences the replenishment of the pools nearer the membrane, that is, the RRP (Kidokoro et al., 2004) and/or the recycling pool (Ratnayaka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a proposal based on the authors' data and citations to previous research.

claim: All the vesicle pools are dynamic and interdependent.
source: All the vesicle pools are dynamic and interdependent (Chamberland and Tóth, 2016; Chanaday et al., 2019), and previous work in Drosophila has shown that impaired recruitment of SVs from the RP to the RRP causes memory deficits and limited short-term synaptic plasticity (Kidokoro et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Impaired recruitment of SVs from the RP to the RRP causes memory deficits and limited short-term synaptic plasticity in Drosophila.
source: All the vesicle pools are dynamic and interdependent (Chamberland and Tóth, 2016; Chanaday et al., 2019), and previous work in Drosophila has shown that impaired recruitment of SVs from the RP to the RRP causes memory deficits and limited short-term synaptic plasticity (Kidokoro et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Modulation of the RP itself, in size or dynamicity, has been shown to affect plasticity and memory.
source: Modulation of the RP itself, in size or dynamicity, has also been shown to affect plasticity and memory (Corradi et al., 2008; De Rossi et al., 2020; Gitler et al., 2008; Skorobogatko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Motor skill learning is usually attributed to the dorsomedial striatum (DMS).
source: We found that lowering KIF1A levels within M1 neurons that project mainly to the DLS rescued motor skill learning, a process that is usually attributed to the dorsomedial striatum (DMS) (Costa et al., 2004; Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent studies have suggested that both DMS and DLS are engaged in learning.
source: Recent studies have suggested that both DMS and DLS are engaged in learning (Bergstrom et al., 2018; Gremel and Costa, 2013; Kimchi et al., 2009; Kupferschmidt et al., 2017; Perez et al., 2022; Perrin and Venance, 2019; Stalnaker et al., 2010; Thorn et al., 2010), so targeting the DLS might be sufficient to rescue the development of motor skill during the first days of rotarod training.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: During consolidation, the number of neurons that are activated upon stimulation of the DLS falls as the circuit streamlines its connections.
source: Rather, this could be related to the observation that during consolidation, the number of neurons that are activated upon stimulation of the DLS falls as the circuit streamlines its connections (Badreddine et al., 2022; Cao et al., 2015; Picard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.
